idiom_name: serialised async methods (promise-chain mutex, e.g. async-mutex)
implementation_notes: TypeScript runs on the same single-threaded agent model as JavaScript, so run-to-completion already serialises synchronous method bodies and the type system adds no runtime primitive; the monitor reappears as an async mutex - a typed promise-chain or queue that serialises the object's async methods, with the async-mutex package as the common off-the-shelf form. Types help express the contract (a Mutex interface, a serialised method signature returning Promise<T>) but cannot enforce that every path takes the lock, and blocking is impossible on the main thread because Atomics.wait throws there. Use it for async resources being shared by concurrent handlers, and message passing for anything that can be handed to a worker.
pitfalls: TypeScript erases to JavaScript: structural typing does not stop a caller from touching the guarded state, so the mutex must be private and every public method must route through it.

A serialised async method must re-validate state after await, because another queued method may have run in between; keeping the invariant inside one synchronous region avoids the whole class of bugs.
Atomics.wait is main-thread-illegal and SharedArrayBuffer needs cross-origin isolation in browsers or worker_threads in Node, so a blocking monitor is only available inside workers.

variants.name: Shared-memory monitor with Atomics across workers
variants.idiom_name: Int32Array lock word + Atomics.wait/notify as monitor lock and condition
variants.implementation_notes: Across agents the only shared mutable memory is a SharedArrayBuffer, so a real monitor is built from Atomics: an Int32Array lock word acquired with a compareExchange spin (parking on Atomics.wait while held) is the monitor lock, and Atomics.wait on a state word plus Atomics.notify is the monitor condition; TypeScript types the views (Int32Array, BigInt64Array) and the Atomics overloads. This is the one blocking monitor available to JavaScript runtimes - inside workers only - and it requires the participating agents to share the buffer, so choose message passing whenever ownership can be transferred.
pitfalls: Atomics.wait throws where blocking is disallowed (the main thread), so the block must live in a worker and the UI thread must use Atomics.waitAsync or message passing.
TypedArray views must share the same buffer; a copied array or a non-shared buffer silently provides no synchronisation, and the lock word must be released on every path.
Atomics.wait also returns on spurious wakeups and timeouts, so predicates must be re-checked in a loop, and stale lock words from a crashed worker wedge the monitor permanently.
